titre: Before 1912, American films were registered for copyright as photographs
accroche: Until August 24, 1912, American law did not recognize film. Producers registered it in the form of photographs.
contenu_vulgarise:
On April 14, 1894, at 1155 Broadway in New York, the Holland brothers' Kinetoscope Parlor opens the first paid public showing of films. Very quickly, making films becomes a competitive business, and producers look for ways to protect themselves from copying. There is a problem: U.S. copyright law makes no provision for registering a film as such. It would not be amended on this point until August 24, 1912.

## A film declared as a photograph

In the meantime, the only open route is to register the film as a series of photographs. The Copyright Office therefore records films in its registers of photographs. Over the years, its classification of these photographs changes, from class D in 1900 to class H in 1901 and then class J in 1909, and those are the headings under which films from 1894 to 1912 must be sought.

The earliest registered film, according to the catalog the Library of Congress published in 1953, is the Kinetoscopic Record of a Sneeze, which Dickson registered on January 7, 1894: the “Fred Ott's Sneeze” of film histories. There are then only three other registrations through the end of 1894, followed by a gap until October 23, 1896, when registrations truly resume.

## What the deposits contain

What producers deposit varies. The Library found Mutoscope reels, frames taken from each scene, production stills, flip-book booklets, and above all entire films printed frame by frame on long rolls of positive photographic paper, the “paper prints.” About half of the films in the catalog are represented in this paper collection.

Howard Lamarr Walls, who is preparing the catalog, has to search more than five hundred official registers, of about two thousand entries each, roughly a million lines, to determine which ones describe a film and which describe a photograph. According to Wikipedia, it is the same Walls who, in 1939, finds more than three thousand of these rolls in a vault of the Copyright Office. In 1953, he writes that an ingenious way has been found to rephotograph them onto celluloid by optical printing so they can be put back into use. Also according to Wikipedia, the Academy funds this work from that same year, and Kemp Niver carries it out over about ten years.

## What this changes

The law had not provided for films, and it is this gap that produced their archive: entire films preserved, frame by frame, on a medium no archivist would have chosen for cinema. The paper survived because the law required a deposit, not because anyone was thinking of film's memory. Walls notes, moreover, that the register does not cover everything, even though it contains the great majority of the films of those eighteen years: not all of them are represented by a roll of paper. What remains are those that do not appear in the register.

repere.texte: American copyright law did not provide for registering films as such before August 24, 1912. The Library of Congress's 1953 catalog had to comb through about a million entries in registers of photographs to identify the films registered between 1894 and 1912.
repere.source: Walls, Motion Pictures 1894-1912, Library of Congress, Copyright Office, 1953, preface

carte.punch: Before 1912, American films were registered for copyright as photographs.
carte.idee: American law did not provide for registering films until 1912. Before that, producers registered them as photographs, sometimes on rolls of paper. Half of the films in the Library of Congress's 1953 catalog appear in its collection of paper rolls.

quiz.question: Why do American films from 1894 to 1912 exist as paper rolls at the Library of Congress?
choix: Because the law made no provision for registering a film, so it was deposited as a series of photographs
Because archivists of the time preferred paper to celluloid, which they considered too fragile
Because producers refused to hand over their negatives and sent only paper copies
Because the 1912 law required each film to be deposited as printed photographs
quiz.explication: Before August 24, 1912, American copyright law recognized only photography: producers therefore deposited their films in that form. The 1912 law precisely put an end to this practice by covering films, and nothing in the sources mentions a choice by archivists or a refusal by producers.
